title: Library management system design
idea: A library management system is a low-level design (LLD) exercise: model copies, members and loans, put the lending rules in one service, and inject storage, policy and time.
points: Lend a `BookCopy`, not a `Book`: three copies of one title are three loans.
`LendingService` owns the rules; repositories only store and find, behind interfaces.
Limits and fines vary, so inject them as policies (the Strategy pattern from c08).
Each rule failure is a `LibraryException` subclass with a stable `code()` for clients.

messages.label: borrow(ada, "C2")
messages.note: The desk app calls one method. It knows nothing about storage or limits.

messages.label: findById("C2")
messages.note: First rule: the copy must exist. The repository answers with an `Optional`, never null.

messages.label: Optional[C2]
messages.note: Found. An empty `Optional` would become `COPY_NOT_FOUND` through `orElseThrow`.

messages.label: forCopy("C2")
messages.note: Second rule: one copy, one active loan. The service asks whether C2 is out.

messages.label: Optional.empty
messages.note: Nobody holds C2, so the copy is free.

messages.label: maxLoans(ada)
messages.note: Third rule: the limit comes from the injected policy, not from a constant in the service.
Ada is not staff, so her limit is two loans.

messages.label: countFor("m-ada")
messages.note: The service counts Ada's active loans.
She already holds C1 and C3, so she is at her limit.

messages.label: throws LOAN_LIMIT
messages.note: The service throws `LoanLimitException`. Nothing was saved, and the desk shows a message for that code.

code.title: Borrowing
code.caption: Entities as records, rules in one service, storage and policy injected, failures with stable codes.

walk.text: Entities are immutable records. A `Loan` links one copy to one member.
Storage and the limit rule are interfaces, so tests and databases can swap in.
One base exception; each subclass fixes its `code()`, which clients may switch on safely.
`borrow` checks exist, free, under limit, in that order, and saves only when all pass.
The in-memory store is not thread-safe. Two desks could lend one copy; a database constraint prevents that.
`main` is the composition root: it builds the stock, picks a policy and runs each case.

code.title: Returns and fines
code.caption: The return side: here `Loan` also carries its due date, which `borrow` would set from the clock and policy. A fixed clock makes fines testable, and a fine policy swaps without editing the service.

walk.text: `FinePolicy` is a strategy. `DailyFine` charges per day up to a cap and rejects negatives.
`giveBack` removes the loan or throws `NOT_ON_LOAN`, then prices lateness from the injected clock.
`Math.max` clamps early returns to zero late days, so no one earns a negative fine.
Each loan tests one case: on time, a few days late, and far past the cap.
Returning C2 twice fails with a code, not a silent second receipt.
An amnesty is a new policy, a lambda here. `ReturnService` does not change.

pitfalls: Modelling `Book` with an `available` flag breaks once the library owns two copies.
Reading `LocalDate.now()` inside the service makes fine tests depend on the calendar.
Check-then-save in `borrow` races under concurrent desks; lock it or rely on a unique constraint.

quiz.q: The library adds a rule: members with unpaid fines cannot borrow. Where does it belong?
options: In the desk app, before calling borrow
In LendingService.borrow, through an injected collaborator
quiz.why: Lending rules live in one service. A copy record knows no members, a repository only stores, and a desk-only check is skipped by other clients.

takeaway: Records for data, one service for rules, interfaces for everything that varies.
